question.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2} \\ {u}^{2}-{v}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 2v \\ 2u & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2v)-2v\cdot 2u \\  & =-4uv-4uv \\  & =-8uv.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ -8uv & =0 \\ uv & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $uv=0$ defines the pair of intersecting lines $u=0$ and $v=0$ in the $uv$-plane. Notice that these lines correspond to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}.$ 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 2v \\ 2u & -2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u\cdot (-2v)-2v\cdot 2u \\  & =-4uv-4uv \\  & =-8uv.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ -8uv & =0 \\ uv & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $uv=0$ defines the pair of intersecting lines $u=0$ and $v=0$ in the $uv$-plane. Notice that these lines correspond to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane.

question.html:
Question 9
?

Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation T, where T is defined as

T:[uv]⟶[u2+v2u2−v2].

a
The critical points lie on the lines u+v=1.
b
The critical points lie on the line u−v=1.
c
The critical points lie on the lines u=0 and v=0.
d
The critical points lie on the line u=−v.
e
The critical points lie on the line u=v.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

To find the locations of the critical points of T, we need to solve ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0.

Here, we have x(u,v)=u2+v2 and y(u,v)=u2−v2.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=2u∂x∂v=2v∂y∂u=2u∂y∂v=−2v

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|2u2v2u−2v|=2u⋅(−2v)−2v⋅2u=−4uv−4uv=−8uv.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0−8uv=0uv=0.

The equation uv=0 defines the pair of intersecting lines u=0 and v=0 in the uv-plane. Notice that these lines correspond to the coordinate axes in the uv-plane.

solution.reasoning: The Jacobian matrix has rows (2u,2v) and (2u,-2v), so its determinant is -8uv. It vanishes exactly when u=0 or v=0; thus the critical set is the union of both coordinate axes. No Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

Question 9

Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation T, where T is defined as

T:[uv]⟶[u2+v2u2−v2].

a
The critical points lie on the lines u+v=1.
b
The critical points lie on the line u−v=1.
c
The critical points lie on the lines u=0 and v=0.
d
The critical points lie on the line u=−v.
e
The critical points lie on the line u=v.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

To find the locations of the critical points of T, we need to solve ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0.

Here, we have x(u,v)=u2+v2 and y(u,v)=u2−v2.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=2u∂x∂v=2v∂y∂u=2u∂y∂v=−2v

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|2u2v2u−2v|=2u⋅(−2v)−2v⋅2u=−4uv−4uv=−8uv.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0−8uv=0uv=0.

The equation uv=0 defines the pair of intersecting lines u=0 and v=0 in the uv-plane. Notice that these lines correspond to the coordinate axes in the uv-plane.

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}uv \\ u+v\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=uv$ and $y(u,v)=u+v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & u \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot 1-u\cdot 1 \\  & =v-u.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ v-u & =0 \\ v & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $v=u$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane.

question.html:
Question 10
?

Find the locations of all of the critical points of T, where T is defined as

T:[uv]⟶[uvu+v].

a
The critical points lie on the line v=u.
b
The critical points lie on the line v=0.
c
The critical points lie on the line u=0.
d
The critical points lie on the circle u2+v2=1.
e
The critical points lie on the hyperbola u2−v2=1.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

To find the locations of the critical points of T, we need to solve ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0.

Here, we have x(u,v)=uv and y(u,v)=u+v.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂x∂u=v∂x∂v=u∂y∂u=1∂y∂v=1

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|=|vu11|=v⋅1−u⋅1=v−u.

The function has critical points when ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0. So, we obtain

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=0v−u=0v=u.

The equation v=u defines a line in the uv-plane.

feedback.name: Question 10
feedback.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}uv \\ u+v\end{aligned}].
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve 

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)=uv$ and $y(u,v)=u+v.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}v & u \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =v\cdot 1-u\cdot 1 \\  & =v-u.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\ v-u & =0 \\ v & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $v=u$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane.

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2xy \\ \frac{y}{x}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=2xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{y}{x}.$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =2x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2y & 2x \\ -\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2y\cdot \frac{1}{x}-2x\cdot (-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{4y}{x} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{y}{x} \\  & =4v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4v}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 11
?

Consider all non-critical points of the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[2xyyx].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T in terms of u and v.

a
2u
b
4v
c
14v
d
−12v
e
−4v
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1.

Here, we have u(x,y)=2xy and v(x,y)=yx.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=2y∂u∂y=2x∂v∂x=−yx2∂v∂y=1x

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|2y2x−yx21x|=2y⋅1x−2x⋅(−yx2)=4yx=4⋅yx=4v.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=14v

last_observation.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=2xy$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{y}{x}.$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2y & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =2x \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2y & 2x \\ -\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2y\cdot \frac{1}{x}-2x\cdot (-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{4y}{x} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{y}{x} \\  & =4v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4v}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2y & 2x \\ -\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}| \\  & =2y\cdot \frac{1}{x}-2x\cdot (-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{4y}{x} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{y}{x} \\  & =4v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4v}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\ x+y\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ and $v(x,y)=x+y.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\cdot 1-(-2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})\cdot 1 \\  & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}+2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =2\cdot (x+y)\cdot {e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =2uv.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2uv}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ and $v(x,y)=x+y.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} & -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\cdot 1-(-2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})\cdot 1 \\  & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}+2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =2\cdot (x+y)\cdot {e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =2uv.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2uv}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12
?

Consider all non-critical points of the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[ex2−y2x+y].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T in terms of u and v.

a
v2u
b
2vu
c
12uv
d
2uv
e
u2v
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1.

Here, we have u(x,y)=ex2−y2 and v(x,y)=x+y.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=2xex2−y2∂u∂y=2yex2−y2∂v∂x=1∂v∂y=1

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|2xex2−y2−2yex2−y211|=2xex2−y2⋅1−(−2yex2−y2)⋅1=2xex2−y2+2yex2−y2=2⋅(x+y)⋅ex2−y2=2uv.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=12uv

solution.reasoning: For the inverse map, u_x=2xu, u_y=-2yu, and v_x=v_y=1. Its Jacobian determinant is 2xu+2yu=2u(x+y)=2uv. At non-critical points it is nonzero, so the Jacobian determinant of T is its reciprocal, 1/(2uv). No Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

Consider all non-critical points of the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[ex2−y2x+y].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T in terms of u and v.

a
v2u
b
2vu
c
12uv
d
2uv

u2v
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1.

Here, we have u(x,y)=ex2−y2 and v(x,y)=x+y.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=2xex2−y2∂u∂y=2yex2−y2∂v∂x=1∂v∂y=1

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|2xex2−y2−2yex2−y211|=2xex2−y2⋅1−(−2yex2−y2)⋅1=2xex2−y2+2yex2−y2=2⋅(x+y)⋅ex2−y2=2uv.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=12uv

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
Consider the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by 

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}5x-4y \\ 2x+3y\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$
question.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

   

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=5x-4y$ and $v(x,y)=2x+3y.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =5 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-4 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot 3-(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =23.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{23}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|5−423|=5⋅3−(−4)⋅2=23.

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=123.

T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)=2x+-y$ and $v(x,y)=x+3y.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-6 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -6 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 3-(-6)\cdot 1 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Consider all non-critical points of the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[exyyx].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T in terms of u and v.

a
−vu
b
4v
c
1v
d
uv
e
12uv
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1.

Here, we have u(x,y)=exy and v(x,y)=yx.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=yexy∂u∂y=xexy∂v∂x=−yx2∂v∂y=1x

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|yexyxexy−yx21x|=yexy⋅1x−xexy⋅(−yx2)=2yexyx=2⋅exy⋅yx=2uv.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=12uv

question.html:
Question 15
?

Consider all non-critical points of the transformation T:(u,v)→(x(u,v),y(u,v)). The inverse transformation T−1(x,y)→(u(x,y),v(x,y)) is given by

T−1:[xy]⟶[exyyx].

Find the Jacobian determinant of T in terms of u and v.

a
−vu
b
4v
c
1v
d
uv
e
12uv
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a transformation

T:[uv]→[x(u,v)y(u,v)],

the Jacobian determinant of T, denoted ∂(x,y)∂(u,v), is given by

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=|∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v|.

In this case, we're only given T−1. So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of T as follows:

  • First, we compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y), the Jacobian determinant of T−1.

  • Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of T using the relation ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1.

Here, we have u(x,y)=exy and v(x,y)=yx.

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂u∂x=yexy∂u∂y=xexy∂v∂x=−yx2∂v∂y=1x

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

∂(u,v)∂(x,y)=|∂u∂x∂u∂y∂v∂x∂v∂y|=|yexyxexy−yx21x|=yexy⋅1x−xexy⋅(−yx2)=2yexyx=2⋅exy⋅yx=2uv.

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=(∂(u,v)∂(x,y))−1=12uv
question.knowledge_point: Jacobian Determinants of Inverse Transformations

solution.reasoning: For the inverse map, u_x=yu, u_y=xu, v_x=-y/x², and v_y=1/x. Its Jacobian determinant is (yu)/x−(xu)(−y/x²)=2u(y/x)=2uv. At non-critical points, the Jacobian determinant of T is the reciprocal, 1/(2uv). No Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

feedback.problem:
Consider all non-critical points of the transformation $T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y)\to (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{y}{x}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have $u(x,y)={e}^{xy}$ and $v(x,y)=\frac{y}{x}.$ 

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =y{e}^{xy} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =x{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}y{e}^{xy} & x{e}^{xy} \\ -\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}| \\  & =y{e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{1}{x}-x{e}^{xy}\cdot (-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{2y{e}^{xy}}{x} \\  & =2\cdot {e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{y}{x} \\  & =2uv.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2uv}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Which of the following sets are open?

I. $\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }0<y<{x}^{2},\,0<x<1\}$

II. $\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }1\le x\le 4,\,1\le {y}^{2}\le 4\}$

III. $\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}:\text{ }0\le x\le 3,\,-1\le y\le 1\}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Let's examine our sets in turn.

- The first set is *open* since it doesn't contain any of its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are strict).

- The second set is *closed* since it contains all of its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are not strict).

- The third set is *closed* since it contains all of its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are not strict).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Which of the following sets are neither open nor closed?

I. $\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le {y}^{2}\le 4\}$

II. $\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<9,\,0\le x\le 3\}$

III. $\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0\le y<\sqrt{x},\,1\le x\le 4\}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Let's examine our sets in turn.

- The first set is *closed* since it contains all its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are not strict).

- The second set is *neither open nor closed*. It contains some of its boundary points, for example, the point $(0,0).$ On the other hand, it does not contain some other boundary points, for example, the point $(3,0).$

- The third set is *neither open nor closed*. It contains some of its boundary points, for example, the point $(1,0).$ On the other hand, it does not contain some other boundary points, for example, the point $(4,2).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Which of the following sets are neither open nor closed?

I. $\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,1\le x<2,\,2<y<4\}$

II. $\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<1\}$

III. $\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Let's examine our sets in turn.

- The first set is *neither open nor closed*. It contains some of its boundary points, for example, the point $(1,3).$ On the other hand, it does not contain some other boundary points, for example, the point $(2,3).$

- The second set is *open* since it doesn't contain any of its boundary points (the corresponding inequality is strict).

- The third set is *closed* since it contains all its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are not strict).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: The solution to the equation $x+4=16$ is $x=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
If we substitute $x=12$ into the given equation, we get a true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4 & =16 \\ 12+4 & =16 \\ 16 & =16\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=12.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
An **equation** consists of two mathematical expressions separated by an equals $(=)$ sign. The expressions may or may not contain variables. Two examples of equations are shown below:

$$
2 + 3 = 5 \qquad\qquad 2 + x = 5
$$

 

An equation is **true** if the expression to the left side of the equals sign is equal to the expression on the right side. Otherwise, if the left side is not equal to the right side, then the equation is **false**. For instance,

- the equation $2 + 3 = 5$ is **true**, whereas

- the equation $2+2 = 5$ is **false**.

As a result, the equation

$$
2 + x = 5
$$

is true *only if* $x=3.$ We say that $x=3$ is the **solution** to the equation $2+x=5.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨6,2,0⟩,$ $⟨-3,5,6⟩,$ and $⟨-1,2,7⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

1.?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨6,2,0⟩, ⟨−3,5,6⟩, and ⟨−1,2,7⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Given that $\{i,j\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ and that the images of $i$ and $j$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨-1,2⟩$ and $⟨3,-8⟩$, respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & -8\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨1,-1,3⟩,$ $⟨-4,3,5⟩,$ and $⟨0,-3,1⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -3 \\ 3 & 5 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Given that $\{i,j\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ and that the images of $i$ and $j$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨-4,3⟩$ and $⟨5,0⟩$, respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.raw_html:
4.?

Given that {i,j} is the standard basis of R2 and that the images of i and j under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨−4,3⟩ and ⟨5,0⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨1,-4,-1⟩,$ $⟨-3,-2,5⟩,$ and $⟨1,0,0⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 & 0 \\ -1 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/2f0c94bc3100b4fd9754ee822f55e2edbae8475bece3b18ac34f63e6c92267a2.png)

In the diagram above, $i$ and $j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$, while ${i}^{′}$ and ${j}^{′}$ are their images under the linear transformation $T.$
What is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/20aff9b0dd1ea6aaab8cfa932317e83015956ac355349d5ae3d744de289bdae5.png)

In the diagram above, $i$ and $j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$, while ${i}^{′}$ and ${j}^{′}$ are their images under the linear transformation $T.$
What is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/5aaf29ab4dd2de3d104ca37a71ee66078f985b908465a77ca06ba8ffadd50210.png)

In the diagram above,  $i$ and $j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$, while ${i}^{′}$ and  ${j}^{′}$ are their images under the linear transformation $T.$
What is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j,k\}$ of ${R}^{3}$ under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ are the first, second, and third columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i,$ $T\cdot j,$ and $T\cdot k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T\cdot k=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j,k\}$ of ${R}^{3}$ under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ are the first, second, and third columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i,$ $T\cdot j,$ and $T\cdot k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T\cdot k=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 
What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j\}$ of ${R}^{2}$ under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i$ and $T\cdot j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

 
What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j\}$ of ${R}^{2}$ under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i$ and $T\cdot j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 
What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j\}$ of ${R}^{2}$ under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i$ and $T\cdot j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.raw_html:
15.?

The linear transformation T has the standard matrix T=[4−451]. What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors {i,j} of R2 under the action of T?

E

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf k\}$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the images of $\mathbf{i},$ $\mathbf{j},$ and $\mathbf{k}$ under the action of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ are
$\langle 3, 5, -1 \rangle,$ $\langle 0, 4,3 \rangle,$ and $\langle -1, 5, -2\rangle,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in $\mathbb{R}^3$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j},$ and $\mathbf k$ under the action of the transformation.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given a Diagram
canonical_examples.problem:
In the diagram below, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$, while $\mathbf{i'}$ and $\mathbf{j'}$ are their images under the linear transformation $\mathbf T.$
What is the standard matrix of $\mathbf T?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/4d1b9e56c0c6214d949d12f45fe4aecea5516971203724ecf573a2b17c6e959a.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that

- the image of $\mathbf{i}$ is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/95f30188b01782a32f4dbfdf48aae31e06846b0faa4a6f741e921ad64910221b.svg) and

- the image of $\mathbf{j}$ is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/0f695a9b9d87ca060eb5011b616d77b7e7d8d9394de6d537a2f2aab759c26a86.svg)

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining the Images of the Standard Basis Vectors Under a Given Linear Transformation
canonical_examples.problem:
The linear transformation $\mathbf T$ has the standard matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/6a14933078db8802426a1ab22ba692e17fd6f795ec4bd746a6fb16687aa441ed.svg) 
What are the images of the standard basis vectors $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under the action of $\mathbf T?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot\mathbf{i}$ and $T\cdot\mathbf{j}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To construct the standard matrix of a linear transformation $T$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ we find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under $T,$ and then use those images as columns in the standard matrix.

To demonstrate, let's consider the following linear transformation: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/b399f02949935d4a4425b19e4946a3eb47375272bb0271586c93da504ff0bd2e.svg)

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf i),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\ 1+3\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf j),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1 \\ 0+3\cdot 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/be0afb6703a6d5e4bcbb360297240a74f4aeec7efbbb1229c8cd01e112fa6bda.svg)

In the diagram below, we see the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and their images $\{ \mathbf{i'}, \mathbf{j'} \}$ under the transformation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/9189a79fe44936221e38e7c051f9f0ddd53338c80cd324ba804d61beef6c2c44.png)

In general, a linear transformation in $\mathbb R^n$ has a standard matrix of dimensions $n \times n,$ whose columns are the images of the basis vectors under the action of the linear transformation.

tutorials.content:
To construct the standard matrix of a linear transformation $T$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ we find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under $T,$ and then use those images as columns in the standard matrix.

To demonstrate, let's consider the following linear transformation: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/b399f02949935d4a4425b19e4946a3eb47375272bb0271586c93da504ff0bd2e.svg)

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf i),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\ 1+3\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf j),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1 \\ 0+3\cdot 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/be0afb6703a6d5e4bcbb360297240a74f4aeec7efbbb1229c8cd01e112fa6bda.svg)

In the diagram below, we see the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and their images $\{ \mathbf{i'}, \mathbf{j'} \}$ under the transformation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/9189a79fe44936221e38e7c051f9f0ddd53338c80cd324ba804d61beef6c2c44.png)

In general, a linear transformation in $\mathbb R^n$ has a standard matrix of dimensions $n \times n,$ whose columns are the images of the basis vectors under the action of the linear transformation.

tutorial.content:
To construct the standard matrix of a linear transformation $T$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ we find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under $T,$ and then use those images as columns in the standard matrix.

To demonstrate, let's consider the following linear transformation: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/ff83f844bbeb50d9404bdd069e0626d448181a6eb8547b8e27af5da577fa46ec.svg)

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf i),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\ 1+3\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf j),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1 \\ 0+3\cdot 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/a3254321a9703ee10ff3dd9bd33cf9511e84abd65fe4ddab7908367c7f7669ac.svg)

In the diagram below, we see the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and their images $\{ \mathbf{i'}, \mathbf{j'} \}$ under the transformation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14156544/assets/9189a79fe44936221e38e7c051f9f0ddd53338c80cd324ba804d61beef6c2c44.png)

In general, a linear transformation in $\mathbb R^n$ has a standard matrix of dimensions $n \times n,$ whose columns are the images of the basis vectors under the action of the linear transformation.

question.problem:
Given that $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf k\}$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the images of $\mathbf{i},$ $\mathbf{j},$ and $\mathbf{k}$ under the action of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ are
$\langle 3, 5, -1 \rangle,$ $\langle 0, 4,3 \rangle,$ and $\langle -1, 5, -2\rangle,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}?$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨6,2,0⟩,$ $⟨-3,5,6⟩,$ and $⟨-1,2,7⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨6,2,0⟩, ⟨−3,5,6⟩, and ⟨−1,2,7⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
[−127−356620]
b
[620−356−127]
c
[0676−3−1252]
d
[0672526−3−1]
e
[6−3−1252067]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R3 can be represented as a 3×3 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i,j, and k under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is T=[6−3−1252067].
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & -8\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ and that the images of $i$ and $j$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨-1,2⟩$ and $⟨3,-8⟩$, respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & -8\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Given that {i,j} is the standard basis of R2 and that the images of i and j under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨−1,2⟩ and ⟨3,−8⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
[3−1−82]
b
[3−12−8]
c
[−132−8]
d
[−123−8]
e
[−823−1]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is
T=[−132−8].
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -3 \\ 3 & 5 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨1,-1,3⟩,$ $⟨-4,3,5⟩,$ and $⟨0,-3,1⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -3 \\ 3 & 5 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨1,−1,3⟩, ⟨−4,3,5⟩, and ⟨0,−3,1⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
[−13−33511−40]
b
[1−40351−13−3]
c
[1−40−13−3351]
d
[−4350−311−13]
e
[1−13−4350−31]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R3 can be represented as a 3×3 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i,j, and k under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is T=[1−40−13−3351].
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 5 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Given that {i,j} is the standard basis of R2 and that the images of i and j under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨−4,3⟩ and ⟨5,0⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [−4353]
b
 [53−40]
c
 [3−405]
d
 [−4350]
e
 [−4530]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is T=[−4530].

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 & 0 \\ -1 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨1,-4,-1⟩,$ $⟨-3,-2,5⟩,$ and $⟨1,0,0⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 \\ -4 & -2 & 0 \\ -1 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 5
?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨1,−4,−1⟩, ⟨−3,−2,5⟩, and ⟨1,0,0⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
[1−310−4−250−1]
b
[1−31−4−20−150]
c
[−4−201−31−150]
d
[1−4−1−3−25100]
e
[1−4−1100−3−25]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R3 can be represented as a 3×3 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i,j, and k under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is T=[1−31−4−20−150].

observed_steps.name: Question 6
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given a Diagram
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

In the diagram above, $i$ and $j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$, while ${i}^{′}$ and ${j}^{′}$ are their images under the linear transformation $T.$
What is the standard matrix of $T?$

question.html:
Question 6
?

In the diagram above, i and j are the vectors of the standard basis of R2, while i′ and j′ are their images under the linear transformation T. What is the standard matrix of T?

a
[123−3]
b
[312−3]
c
[31−32]
d
[3−312]
e
[132−3]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that i′=[3−3] and j′=[12].

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[31−32].

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

[31−12]

[−1231]

[−1321]

[3−121]

[3−112]

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[3−112].

Question 9
?

In the diagram above, i and j are the vectors of the standard basis of R2, while i′ and j′ are their images under the linear transformation T. What is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [21−23]
b
 [−2321]
c
 [−2123]
d
[−2231]
e
 [2−213]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that i′=[−23] and j′=[21].

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[−2231].

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 10
?

In the diagram above, i and j are the vectors of the standard basis of R2, while i′ and j′ are their images under the linear transformation T. What is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [112−1]
b
 [12−1−1]
c
 [−1−112]
d
[1−12−1]
e
[−121−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that i′=[12] and j′=[−1−1].

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[1−12−1].
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given a Diagram

observed_steps.name: Example: Determining the Images of the Standard Basis Vectors Under a Given Linear Transformation
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given a Diagram
observed_steps.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot\mathbf{i}$ and $T\cdot\mathbf{j}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Images of the Standard Basis Vectors Under a Given Linear Transformation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ are the first, second, and third columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i,$ $T\cdot j,$ and $T\cdot k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T\cdot k=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j,k\}$ of ${R}^{3}$ under the action of $T?$

question.html:
Question 11
?

The linear transformation T has the standard matrix T=[1−2341−1110]. What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors {i,j,k} of R3 under the action of T?

a
 [1−23], [41−1], and [110]
b
 [141], [−211], and [3−10]
c
 [123], [41−1], and [110]
d
 [141], [2−11], and [310]
e
 [114], [−211], and [30−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

The images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j,k} are the first, second, and third columns of T, respectively.

Therefore, we have the following:

T(i)=T[100]=[141]T(j)=T[010]=[−211]T(k)=T[001]=[3−10]

Method 2

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j,k} by computing the matrix products T⋅i, T⋅j, and T⋅k:

T(i)=T⋅i=[1−2341−1110][100]=[141]T(j)=T⋅j=[1−2341−1110][010]=[−211]T(k)=T⋅k=[1−2341−1110][001]=[3−10]
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Images of the Standard Basis Vectors Under a Given Linear Transformation

observed_steps.name: Question 12
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Images of the Standard Basis Vectors Under a Given Linear Transformation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ are the first, second, and third columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i,$ $T\cdot j,$ and $T\cdot k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T\cdot k=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j,k\}$ of ${R}^{3}$ under the action of $T?$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i,$ $T\cdot j,$ and $T\cdot k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T\cdot k=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 12
?

The linear transformation T has the standard matrix T=[1−4−1−35−20−10]. What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors {i,j,k} of R3 under the action of T?

a
[−310], [5−4−1], and [−2−10]
b
[1−30], [−45−1], and [−1−20]
c
[−35−2], [1−4−1], and [0−10]
d
[−45−1], [1−30], and [−1−20]
e
[1−4−1], [−35−2], and [0−10]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Method 1

The images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j,k} are the first, second, and third columns of T, respectively.

Therefore, we have the following:

T(i)=T[100]=[1−30]T(j)=T[010]=[−45−1]T(k)=T[001]=[−1−20]

Method 2

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j,k} by computing the matrix products T⋅i, T⋅j, and T⋅k:

T(i)=T⋅i=[1−4−1−35−20−10][100]=[1−30]T(j)=T⋅j=[1−4−1−35−20−10][010]=[−45−1]T(k)=T⋅k=[1−4−1−35−20−10][001]=[−1−20]
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Images of the Standard Basis Vectors Under a Given Linear Transformation

observed_steps.name: Question 13
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Images of the Standard Basis Vectors Under a Given Linear Transformation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i$ and $T\cdot j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 
What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j\}$ of ${R}^{2}$ under the action of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i$ and $T\cdot j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
