questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{4}-{y}^{4}$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,j \\  & =4{x}^{3}\,i-4{y}^{3}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}y)$ and $r(t)=t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}y)\,j \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}y}\,i+\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}y}\,j \\  & =\frac{3}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{3}{t}\,i+\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{3}{t}\,i+\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\,j)\cdot (\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =\frac{3}{t}+\frac{{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{3}{t}+1 \\  & =\frac{t+3}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=\sqrt{xy}$ and $r(t)={t}^{3}\,i+t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xy})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xy})\,j \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{y}}{2\sqrt{x}}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{y}}\,j\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{3}$ and $y=t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}{2\sqrt{t}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{t}{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{t}{2}\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2t}+\frac{t}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}t+\frac{1}{2}t \\  & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)=z(x+y)$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z(x+y))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z(x+y))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z(x+y))\,k \\  & =z\,i+z\,j+(x+y)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & ={e}^{t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)$ and $r(t)=t\,i+2t\,j+\frac{1}{t}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,k \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,i+xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,j+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y=2t$ and $z=\frac{1}{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k)\cdot (\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 2+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)$ and $r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+{e}^{t}\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,k \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,i-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,j+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡z\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y={t}^{2}$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =i+2t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}\,k)\cdot (i+2t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t-2t\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+xz$ and $r(t)=t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+e\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+yz+xz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+yz+xz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+yz+xz)\,k \\  & =(y+z)\,i+(x+z)\,j+(y+x)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,y={e}^{t},$ and $z=e$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(e)\,k \\  & =i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k)\cdot (i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k) \\  & =({e}^{t}+e)\cdot 1+(t+e)\cdot {e}^{t}+({e}^{t}+t)\cdot 0 \\  & ={e}^{t}+e+t{e}^{t}+{e}^{t+1} \\  & ={e}^{t+1}+(1+t){e}^{t}+e.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}$ and $r(t)=(t+1)\,i+(t-1)\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j+4z\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t+1,$ $y=t-1$ and $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2(t+1)\,i+2(t-1)\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =i+j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2(t+1)\,i+2(t-1)\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k)\cdot (i+j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k) \\  & =2(t+1)\cdot 1+2(t-1)\cdot 1+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2t+2+2t-2+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =4(t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=\sqrt{2}$ given that $∇f(x,y)=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+\frac{x}{x+y})i+\frac{x}{x+y}\,j$ and $r(t)=2t\,i+(1-2t)\,j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+\frac{x}{x+y})i+\frac{x}{x+y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=1-2t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1-2t)+\frac{2t}{2t+1-2t})i+\frac{2t}{2t+1-2t}\,j \\  & =2t\,i+2t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)\,j \\  & =2\,i+(-2)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2t\,i+2t\,j)\cdot (2\,i+(-2)\,j) \\  & =2t\cdot 2+2t\cdot (-2) \\  & =4t-4t \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\sqrt{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\sqrt{2}))] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem: Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that $∇f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡y\,i+\frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}\,j$ and $r(t)=({t}^{2}+1)\,i+t\,j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡y\,i+\frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x={t}^{2}+1$ and $y=t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =2t\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+j)\cdot (2t\,i+j) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\cdot 2t+1\cdot 1 \\  & =2t\operatorname{arctan}⁡t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =2(1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+1 \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+1 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem: Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ given that $∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\text{ }i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\text{ }j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem: Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=-1$ given that $∇f(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}\,i+(x{e}^{xy}+2y)\,j$ and $r(t)=(t+1)\,i+(t-1)\,j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}\,i+(x{e}^{xy}+2y)\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=t+1$ and $y=t-1$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(t-1){e}^{(t+1)(t-1)}\,i+((t+1){e}^{(t+1)(t-1)}+2(t-1))\,j \\  & =(t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}\,i+((t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,j \\  & =i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}\,i+((t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2)\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =(t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}\cdot 1+((t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2)\cdot 1 \\  & =(t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+(t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2 \\  & =2t{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=-1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(-1))] & =2(-1){e}^{(-1)^{2}-1}+2(-1)-2 \\  & =-2-2-2 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem: Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ given that $∇f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i+x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,j$ and $r(t)=\frac{t}{2}\,i+t\,j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i+x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=\frac{t}{2}$ and $y=t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\frac{t}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\frac{t}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\,i+j) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \frac{1}{2}+\frac{t}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{2}))] & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1+\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\frac{1}{t},t⟩$ at the point $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z)),\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z))⟩ \\  & =⟨-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy+z),-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy+z),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy+z)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=\frac{1}{t},$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\cdot ⟨2t,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},1⟩ \\  & =(-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot 2t+(-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot 1 \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+3xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},t+1,-t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+3xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x+3yz,3xz,3xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=t+1,$ and $z=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2({t}^{2})+3(t+1)(-t),3({t}^{2})(-t),3({t}^{2})(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2}-3{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2t,1,-1⟩ \\  & =(-{t}^{2}-3t)\cdot 2t+(-3{t}^{3})\cdot 1+(3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2})\cdot (-1) \\  & =-2{t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} \\  & =-8{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =-8{(1)}^{3}-9{(1)}^{2}=-17.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 18
questions.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,3t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(x+y)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(x+y)^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=3t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(2t+3t)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(2t+3t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(5t)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(5t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}},\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}},\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨2,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{5}{1+25{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{5}{1+25(1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{1+25} \\  & =\frac{5}{26}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 19
questions.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{y}+z$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨4,\operatorname{ln}⁡t,{e}^{t}⟩$ at the point $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+z),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+z),\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}+z)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{y},x{e}^{y},1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=4,$ $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t},4{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t},1⟩ \\  & =⟨t,4t,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\frac{1}{t},{e}^{t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨t,4t,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\frac{1}{t},{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =t\cdot 0+4t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+1\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =4+{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(2))] & =4+{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 20
questions.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2\sqrt{t},4t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2\sqrt{t}$ and $y=4t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},4⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)\cdot 4 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{1}-4\cdot 1)(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}-4) \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Two Variables
canonical_examples.problem: If $f(x,y) = x^2 + 2 y^3$ and $\mathbf r (t) = \sin t \ \mathbf i + e^{t} \ \mathbf j,$ compute $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r(t))].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{3})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{3})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+6{y}^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x = \sin t$ and $y=e^{t}$  into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+6({e}^{t})^{2}\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6{e}^{2t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\text{ }i+6{e}^{2t}\text{ }j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\text{ }i+{e}^{t}\text{ }j) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6{e}^{2t}\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+6{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Two Variables

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Applying the Vector Form of the Chain Rule to a Function of Three Variables
canonical_examples.problem: If $f(x,y,z) = xz\ln{y}$ and $\mathbf r (t) =  t^2 \, \mathbf i + t  \, \mathbf j +t^3  \, \mathbf k,$ compute $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r(t))].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xz\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xz\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xz\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,k \\  & =z\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,i+\frac{xz}{y}\,j+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x= t^2,$ $y = t$ and $z= t^3$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+{t}^{4}\,j+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,k \\  & =2t\,i+\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+{t}^{4}\,j+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,k)\cdot (2t\,i+\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k) \\  & =({t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\cdot 2t+({t}^{4})\cdot 1+({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\cdot 3{t}^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡t+{t}^{4}+3{t}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡t \\  & ={t}^{4}(5\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating the Derivative at a Point Using the Chain Rule
canonical_examples.problem:
Evaluate $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t}[f(\mathbf r(t))]$ at $t = \pi$ given that
$\nabla f(x,y) = (2y - 1) \, \mathbf i + (2x-1) \, \mathbf j$
and
$\mathbf r (t) = \sin{t} \, \mathbf i + \cos{t} \, \mathbf j.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = (2y - 1) \, \mathbf i + (2x - 1) \, \mathbf j.
$$

First, we substitute $x = \sin{t}$ and $y = \cos{t}$ into $\nabla f(x,y)$ to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\,i+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1\,i+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2{sin}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t = \pi,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =2(1)+0-(-1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing the Rate of Change of a Multivariable Function at a Point Using the Chain Rule
canonical_examples.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=x^2-y^2-z$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf r (t) = \left \langle \sin t, \cos t, t  \right \rangle$ at the point $t=\dfrac \pi 4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf r (t)$ is given by $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] .$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x,-2y,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x = \sin t, y=\cos t,$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf r(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-1⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-1\cdot 1 \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1 \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-1 \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have the function 

$$
f(\mathbf{r}) = f(x,y) = xy^2,
$$

which takes a vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t) \right\rangle = \left\langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle
$$

as input. How do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right]?$

To do this, we use the **multivariable chain rule in vector form**, which states

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

Let's now apply this to our functions. First, we compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(f(x,y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(f(x,y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨{y}^{2},2xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2},2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =-{sin}^{3}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: The Derivative as a Rate of Change
tutorials.problem:
We can consider $f(\mathbf{r}(t))$ as the values taken by the function $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$ So, the derivative 

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))]
$$

can be interpreted as the **rate of change of $f$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$**

Furthermore, if $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is a level curve $f(x,y)=c,$ then by the chain rule we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =c \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(f(r(t))) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(c) \\ ∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

From this, we can conclude that the gradient vector $\nabla f$ is orthogonal to every level curve of $f.$

tutorials.name: Intuition Behind the Vector Form of the Multivariable Chain Rule
tutorials.problem:
The chain rule for a function $f(\mathbf{r}),$ where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x_1(t), x_2(t), \ldots, x_m(t) \right\rangle$ is a vector-valued function of $m$ variables, is the same as before:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)
$$

How does this chain rule in vector form relate to the chain rule we have seen before, which states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d f} {\textrm d t} 	= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_1}{\textrm d t}  
						+ \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_2}{\textrm d t} + \dots + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_m}{\textrm d t}?
$$

Let's expand $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$ to see. Recall that 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))=⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩ \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{\text{d}t}+⋯+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

They are exactly the same, just different notations!

**Note**: If we replace $\mathbf{r}$ with a single-valued function $g(t),$ we get back the chain rule from single-variable calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(g(t))] & =∇f(g(t))\cdot {g}^{′}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$
tutorials.content:
The chain rule for a function $f(\mathbf{r}),$ where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x_1(t), x_2(t), \ldots, x_m(t) \right\rangle$ is a vector-valued function of $m$ variables, is the same as before:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)
$$

How does this chain rule in vector form relate to the chain rule we have seen before, which states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d f} {\textrm d t} 	= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_1}{\textrm d t}  
						+ \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_2}{\textrm d t} + \dots + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_m}{\textrm d t}?
$$

Let's expand $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$ to see. Recall that 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))=⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩ \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{\text{d}t}+⋯+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

They are exactly the same, just different notations!

**Note**: If we replace $\mathbf{r}$ with a single-valued function $g(t),$ we get back the chain rule from single-variable calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(g(t))] & =∇f(g(t))\cdot {g}^{′}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorial.problem:
Suppose we have the function 

$$
f(\mathbf{r}) = f(x,y) = xy^2,
$$

which takes a vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x(t), y(t) \right\rangle = \left\langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle
$$

as input. How do we calculate $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right]?$

To do this, we use the **multivariable chain rule in vector form**, which states

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left[f(\mathbf{r}(t))\right] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

Let's now apply this to our functions. First, we compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(f(x,y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(f(x,y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨{y}^{2},2xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2},2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨{sin}^{2}⁡t,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =-{sin}^{3}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(x2+xy)i+∂∂y(x2+xy)j=(2x+y)i+xj

Next, we substitute x=t+1 and y=−t2 into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=(2t+2−t2)i+(t+1)j

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t+1)i+ddt(−t2)j=i−2tj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((2t+2−t2)i+(t+1)j)⋅(i−2tj)=2t+2−t2−2t(t+1)=2t+2−t2−2t2−2t=2−3t2.

question.problem: If $f(x,y)={e}^{x-y}$ and $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i-t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}{e}^{x-y}\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{x-y}\,i-{e}^{x-y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,i-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)\,j \\  & =2t\,i-\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,i-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,j)\cdot (2t\,i-\,j) \\  & ={e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\cdot 2t+(-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t})\cdot (-1) \\  & =(2t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=ex−y and r(t)=t2i−tj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2tet2+t
b
(2t+1)et2+t
c
(t+1)et2−t
d
t2et2−t
e
(t−2)et2+t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂xex−yi+∂∂yex−yj=ex−yi−ex−yj

Next, we substitute x=t2 and y=−t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=et2+ti−et2+tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t2)i+ddt(−t)j=2ti−j.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(et2+ti−et2+tj)⋅(2ti−j)=et2+t⋅2t+(−et2+t)⋅(−1)=(2t+1)et2+t.

Next, we substitute x=t and y=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(et)j=i+etj.

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(3ti+1etj)⋅(i+etj)=3t+etet=3t+1=t+3t.

Next, we substitute x=sin⁡t, y=cos⁡t and z=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=eti+etj+(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)k

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(sin⁡t)i+ddt(cos⁡t)j+ddt(et)k=cos⁡ti−sin⁡tj+etk.

$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k)\cdot (\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 2+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 7
?

If f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(xyz) and r(t)=ti+2tj+1tk, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
4cos⁡(2t)−cos⁡t
b
4cos⁡(2t)
c
cos⁡(2t)+1t
d
2cos⁡(2t)
e
(2+2t)cos⁡(2t)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y,z):

∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂x(sin⁡(xyz))i+∂∂y(sin⁡(xyz))j+∂∂z(sin⁡(xyz))k=yzcos⁡(xyz)i+xzcos⁡(xyz)j+xycos⁡(xyz)k

Next, we substitute x=t, y=2t and z=1t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=2cos⁡(2t)i+cos⁡(2t)j+2t2cos⁡(2t)k

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(2t)j+ddt(1t)k=i+2j−1t2k.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(2cos⁡(2t)i+cos⁡(2t)j+2t2cos⁡(2t)k)⋅(i+2j−1t2k)=2cos⁡(2t)⋅1+cos⁡(2t)⋅2+2t2cos⁡(2t)⋅(−1t2)=2cos⁡(2t)+2cos⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(2t)=2cos⁡(2t).

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,k \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,i-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,j+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡z\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y={t}^{2}$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =i+2t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}\,k)\cdot (i+2t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t-2t\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

If f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(sin⁡xcos⁡ysin⁡z) and r(t)=ti+t2j+etk, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
cot⁡t−2ttan⁡t2+etcot⁡et
b
 2cot⁡t−tan⁡t2
c
 cot⁡et−2tan⁡t2
d
 tcot⁡t+t2tan⁡t2+ettan⁡et
e
 cot⁡t−tan⁡t2+cot⁡et
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y,z): ∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂xln⁡(sin⁡xcos⁡ysin⁡z)i+∂∂yln⁡(sin⁡xcos⁡ysin⁡z)j+∂∂zln⁡(sin⁡xcos⁡ysin⁡z)k=cos⁡xcos⁡ysin⁡zsin⁡xcos⁡ysin⁡zi−sin⁡xsin⁡ysin⁡zsin⁡xcos⁡ysin⁡zj+sin⁡xcos⁡ycos⁡zsin⁡xcos⁡ysin⁡zk=cot⁡xi−tan⁡yj+cot⁡zk

Next, we substitute x=t, y=t2 and z=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=cot⁡ti−tan⁡t2j+cot⁡etk

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(t2)j+ddt(et)k=i+2tj+etk.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(cot⁡ti−tan⁡t2j+cot⁡etk)⋅(i+2tj+etk)=cot⁡t−2ttan⁡t2+etcot⁡et.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+yz+xz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+yz+xz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+yz+xz)\,k \\  & =(y+z)\,i+(x+z)\,j+(y+x)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,y={e}^{t},$ and $z=e$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(e)\,k \\  & =i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k)\cdot (i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k) \\  & =({e}^{t}+e)\cdot 1+(t+e)\cdot {e}^{t}+({e}^{t}+t)\cdot 0 \\  & ={e}^{t}+e+t{e}^{t}+{e}^{t+1} \\  & ={e}^{t+1}+(1+t){e}^{t}+e.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

If f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+xz and r(t)=ti+etj+ek, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
et+1+(1+2t)et+e
b
et+1+(1+t)et+e
c
2et+2e+t
d
et+1+tet+e
e
et+1+(t+1)et+2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y,z):

∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂x(xy+yz+xz)i+∂∂y(xy+yz+xz)j+∂∂z(xy+yz+xz)k=(y+z)i+(x+z)j+(y+x)k

Next, we substitute x=t,y=et, and z=e into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=(et+e)i+(t+e)j+(et+t)k

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(et)j+ddt(e)k=i+etj+(0)k.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((et+e)i+(t+e)j+(et+t)k)⋅(i+etj+(0)k)=(et+e)⋅1+(t+e)⋅et+(et+t)⋅0=et+e+tet+et+1=et+1+(1+t)et+e.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j+4z\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t+1,$ $y=t-1$ and $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2(t+1)\,i+2(t-1)\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =i+j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2(t+1)\,i+2(t-1)\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k)\cdot (i+j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k) \\  & =2(t+1)\cdot 1+2(t-1)\cdot 1+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2t+2+2t-2+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =4(t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12
?

Evaluate ddt[f(r(t))] at t=1 given that ∇f(x,y)=arctan⁡yi+x1+y2j and r(t)=(t2+1)i+tj.

a
π+22
b
π2+1
c
π2
d
1
e
0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

In addition, we've been given that ∇f(x,y)=arctan⁡yi+x1+y2j.

First, we substitute x=t2+1 and y=t into ∇f(x,y) to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=arctan⁡ti+t2+11+t2j=arctan⁡ti+j

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=ddt(t2+1)i+ddt(t)j=2ti+j.

Applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(arctan⁡ti+j)⋅(2ti+j)=arctan⁡t⋅2t+1⋅1=2tarctan⁡t+1.

Finally, evaluating the above at t=1, we obtain ddt[f(r(1))]=2(1)arctan⁡1+1=2⋅π4+1=π2+1=π+22.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,i+\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}\,i+(x{e}^{xy}+2y)\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=t+1$ and $y=t-1$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(t-1){e}^{(t+1)(t-1)}\,i+((t+1){e}^{(t+1)(t-1)}+2(t-1))\,j \\  & =(t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}\,i+((t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,j \\  & =i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}\,i+((t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2)\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =(t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}\cdot 1+((t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2)\cdot 1 \\  & =(t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+(t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2 \\  & =2t{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=-1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(-1))] & =2(-1){e}^{(-1)^{2}-1}+2(-1)-2 \\  & =-2-2-2 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorial.name: The Derivative as a Rate of Change
tutorial.problem:
We can consider $f(\mathbf{r}(t))$ as the values taken by the function $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$ So, the derivative 

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))]
$$

can be interpreted as the **rate of change of $f$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t).$**

Furthermore, if $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is a level curve $f(x,y)=c,$ then by the chain rule we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =c \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(f(r(t))) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(c) \\ ∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

From this, we can conclude that the gradient vector $\nabla f$ is orthogonal to every level curve of $f.$

The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf r (t)$ is given by $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] .$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x,-2y,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x = \sin t, y=\cos t,$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf r(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-1⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,1⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-1\cdot 1 \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1 \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-1 \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16
?

Compute the rate of change of the function f(x,y,z)=cos⁡(xy+z) with respect to t along the curve r(t)=⟨t2,1t,t⟩ at the point t=π4.

a
−2
b
2
c
1
d
−2
e
0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The rate of change of f(x,y,z) with respect to t along the curve r(t) is given by ddt[f(r(t))]. To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=⟨∂∂x(cos⁡(xy+z)),∂∂y(cos⁡(xy+z)),∂∂z(cos⁡(xy+z))⟩=⟨−ysin⁡(xy+z),−xsin⁡(xy+z),−sin⁡(xy+z)⟩

Next, we substitute x=t2,y=1t, and z=t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=⟨−1tsin⁡(2t),−t2sin⁡(2t),−sin⁡(2t)⟩

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=⟨ddt(t2),ddt(1t),ddt(t)⟩=⟨2t,−1t2,1⟩.

Applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=⟨−1tsin⁡(2t),−t2sin⁡(2t),−sin⁡(2t)⟩⋅⟨2t,−1t2,1⟩=(−1tsin⁡(2t))⋅2t+(−t2sin⁡(2t))⋅(−1t2)+(−sin⁡(2t))⋅1=−2sin⁡(2t)+sin⁡(2t)−sin⁡(2t)=−2sin⁡(2t).

Therefore, the rate of change of f along the curve r(t) at t=π4 is

ddt[f(r(π4))]=−2sin⁡(2⋅π4)=−2.

Question 18
?

Compute the rate of change of the function f(x,y)=arctan⁡(x+y) with respect to t along the curve r(t)=⟨2t,3t⟩ at the point t=1.

a
526
b
−213
c
π2−1
d
713
e
π+2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The rate of change of f(x,y,z) with respect to t along the curve r(t) is given by ddt[f(r(t))]. To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y): ∇f(x,y)=⟨∂∂x(arctan⁡(x+y)),∂∂y(arctan⁡(x+y))⟩=⟨11+(x+y)2,11+(x+y)2⟩

Next, we substitute x=2t and y=3t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=⟨11+(2t+3t)2,11+(2t+3t)2⟩=⟨11+(5t)2,11+(5t)2⟩=⟨11+25t2,11+25t2⟩

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=⟨ddt(2t),ddt(3t)⟩=⟨2,3⟩.

Applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=⟨11+25t2,11+25t2⟩⋅⟨2,3⟩=11+25t2⋅2+11+25t2⋅3=51+25t2.

Therefore, the rate of change of f along the curve r(t) at t=1 is ddt[f(r(1))]=51+25(1)2=51+25=526.

The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+z),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+z),\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}+z)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{y},x{e}^{y},1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=4,$ $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t},4{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t},1⟩ \\  & =⟨t,4t,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\frac{1}{t},{e}^{t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨t,4t,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\frac{1}{t},{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =t\cdot 0+4t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+1\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =4+{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(2))] & =4+{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Compute the rate of change of the function f(x,y,z)=xey+z with respect to t along the curve r(t)=⟨4,ln⁡t,et⟩ at the point t=2.

a
0
b
2e2−1
c
4+e2
d
e2−3
e
2

Correct
EXPLANATION

The rate of change of f(x,y,z) with respect to t along the curve r(t) is given by ddt[f(r(t))]. To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y): ∇f(x,y)=⟨∂∂x(xey+z),∂∂y(xey+z),∂∂z(xey+z)⟩=⟨ey,xey,1⟩

Next, we substitute x=4, y=ln⁡t and z=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=⟨eln⁡t,4eln⁡t,1⟩=⟨t,4t,1⟩

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=⟨ddt(4),ddt(ln⁡t),et⟩=⟨0,1t,et⟩.

Applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=⟨t,4t,1⟩⋅⟨0,1t,et⟩=t⋅0+4t⋅1t+1⋅et=4+et.

Therefore, the rate of change of f along the curve r(t) at t=2 is ddt[f(r(2))]=4+e2.

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2\sqrt{t}$ and $y=4t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},4⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)\cdot 4 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{1}-4\cdot 1)(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}-4) \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 20
?

Compute the rate of change of the function f(x,y)=sin⁡(x−y) with respect to t along the curve r(t)=⟨2t,4t⟩ at the point t=1.

a
−3cos⁡2
b
5cos⁡2
c
−3cos⁡8
d
0
e
cos⁡2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The rate of change of f(x,y,z) with respect to t along the curve r(t) is given by ddt[f(r(t))]. To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y): ∇f(x,y)=⟨∂∂x(sin⁡(x−y)),∂∂y(sin⁡(x−y))⟩=⟨cos⁡(x−y),−cos⁡(x−y)⟩

Next, we substitute x=2t and y=4t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=⟨cos⁡(2t−4t),−cos⁡(2t−4t)⟩

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=⟨ddt(2t),ddt(4t)⟩=⟨1t,4⟩.

Applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=⟨cos⁡(2t−4t),−cos⁡(2t−4t)⟩⋅⟨1t,4⟩=cos⁡(2t−4t)⋅1t−cos⁡(2t−4t)⋅4=cos⁡(2t−4t)(1t−4).

Therefore, the rate of change of f along the curve r(t) at t=1 is ddt[f(r(1))]=cos⁡(21−4⋅1)(11−4)=−3cos⁡2.

tutorial.name: Intuition Behind the Vector Form of the Multivariable Chain Rule
tutorial.problem:
The chain rule for a function $f(\mathbf{r}),$ where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle x_1(t), x_2(t), \ldots, x_m(t) \right\rangle$ is a vector-valued function of $m$ variables, is the same as before:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)
$$

How does this chain rule in vector form relate to the chain rule we have seen before, which states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d f} {\textrm d t} 	= \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_1} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm d x_1}{\textrm d t}  
						+ \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_2} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_2}{\textrm d t} + \dots + \dfrac {\partial f}{\partial x_m} \cdot  \dfrac {\textrm d x_m}{\textrm d t}?
$$

Let's expand $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)$ to see. Recall that 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))=⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}},\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}},…,\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{dt},\frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{dt},…,\frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{dt}⟩ \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{1}}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{2}}{\text{d}t}+⋯+\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{m}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{x}_{m}}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

They are exactly the same, just different notations!

**Note**: If we replace $\mathbf{r}$ with a single-valued function $g(t),$ we get back the chain rule from single-variable calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(g(t))] & =∇f(g(t))\cdot {g}^{′}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+xy$ and $r(t)=(t+1)\,i-{t}^{2}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy)\,j \\  & =(2x+y)\,i+x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t+1$ and $y=-{t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2t+2-{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =\,i-2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((2t+2-{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\,j)\cdot (\,i-2t\,j) \\  & =2t+2-{t}^{2}-2t(t+1) \\  & =2t+2-{t}^{2}-2{t}^{2}-2t \\  & =2-3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=x2+xy and r(t)=(t+1)i−t2j, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2−3t2
b
 4t−t2
c
3+3t−t2
d
 2−4t
e
2+4t−3t2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(x2+xy)i+∂∂y(x2+xy)j=(2x+y)i+xj

Next, we substitute x=t+1 and y=−t2 into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=(2t+2−t2)i+(t+1)j

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t+1)i+ddt(−t2)j=i−2tj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((2t+2−t2)i+(t+1)j)⋅(i−2tj)=2t+2−t2−2t(t+1)=2t+2−t2−2t2−2t=2−3t2.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy)\,j \\  & =(2x+y)\,i+x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t+1$ and $y=-{t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2t+2-{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =\,i-2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((2t+2-{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\,j)\cdot (\,i-2t\,j) \\  & =2t+2-{t}^{2}-2t(t+1) \\  & =2t+2-{t}^{2}-2{t}^{2}-2t \\  & =2-3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: If $f(x,y)={e}^{x-y}$ and $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i-t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}{e}^{x-y}\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{x-y}\,i-{e}^{x-y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,i-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)\,j \\  & =2t\,i-\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,i-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,j)\cdot (2t\,i-\,j) \\  & ={e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\cdot 2t+(-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t})\cdot (-1) \\  & =(2t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=ex−y and r(t)=t2i−tj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2tet2+t
b
(2t+1)et2+t
c
(t+1)et2−t
d
t2et2−t
e
(t−2)et2+t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂xex−yi+∂∂yex−yj=ex−yi−ex−yj

Next, we substitute x=t2 and y=−t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=et2+ti−et2+tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t2)i+ddt(−t)j=2ti−j.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(et2+ti−et2+tj)⋅(2ti−j)=et2+t⋅2t+(−et2+t)⋅(−1)=(2t+1)et2+t.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}{e}^{x-y}\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{x-y}\,i-{e}^{x-y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,i-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)\,j \\  & =2t\,i-\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,i-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,j)\cdot (2t\,i-\,j) \\  & ={e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\cdot 2t+(-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t})\cdot (-1) \\  & =(2t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=ex−y and r(t)=t2i−tj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2tet2+t
b
(2t+1)et2+t
c
(t+1)et2−t
d
t2et2−t
e
(t−2)et2+t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂xex−yi+∂∂yex−yj=ex−yi−ex−yj

Next, we substitute x=t2 and y=−t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=et2+ti−et2+tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t2)i+ddt(−t)j=2ti−j.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(et2+ti−et2+tj)⋅(2ti−j)=et2+t⋅2t+(−et2+t)⋅(−1)=(2t+1)et2+t.

\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}{e}^{x-y}\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{x-y}\,i-{e}^{x-y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,i-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)\,j \\  & =2t\,i-\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,i-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,j)\cdot (2t\,i-\,j) \\  & ={e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\cdot 2t+(-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t})\cdot (-1) \\  & =(2t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t2)i+ddt(−t)j=2ti−j.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(et2+ti−et2+tj)⋅(2ti−j)=et2+t⋅2t+(−et2+t)⋅(−1)=(2t+1)et2+t.

question.problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{4}-{y}^{4}$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,j \\  & =4{x}^{3}\,i-4{y}^{3}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

question.problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}y)$ and $r(t)=t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}y)\,j \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}y}\,i+\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}y}\,j \\  & =\frac{3}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{3}{t}\,i+\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{3}{t}\,i+\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\,j)\cdot (\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =\frac{3}{t}+\frac{{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{3}{t}+1 \\  & =\frac{t+3}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

If f(x,y)=ln⁡(x3y) and r(t)=ti+etj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
et+3et
b
3+et
c
tet+3t
d
t+3t
e
3et+ttet
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂xln⁡(x3y)i+∂∂yln⁡(x3y)j=3x2yx3yi+x3x3yj=3xi+1yj

Next, we substitute x=t and y=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=3ti+1etj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(et)j=i+etj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(3ti+1etj)⋅(i+etj)=3t+etet=3t+1=t+3t.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}y)\,j \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}y}\,i+\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}y}\,j \\  & =\frac{3}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{3}{t}\,i+\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{3}{t}\,i+\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\,j)\cdot (\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =\frac{3}{t}+\frac{{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{3}{t}+1 \\  & =\frac{t+3}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

If f(x,y)=ln⁡(x3y) and r(t)=ti+etj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
et+3et
b
3+et
c
tet+3t
d
t+3t
e
3et+ttet
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂xln⁡(x3y)i+∂∂yln⁡(x3y)j=3x2yx3yi+x3x3yj=3xi+1yj

Next, we substitute x=t and y=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=3ti+1etj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(et)j=i+etj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(3ti+1etj)⋅(i+etj)=3t+etet=3t+1=t+3t.

solution.reasoning: For t>0, substitution gives f(r(t))=ln(t^3 e^t)=3 ln(t)+t. Differentiating gives 3/t+1=(t+3)/t, matching option d. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key; the worked example concerns a different problem.
